Major amino acid metabolic pathways involved in aortic diseases

Major amino acid metabolic pathways involved in aortic diseases. This diagram illustrates key interconnected amino acid metabolic networks implicated in aortic pathologies. (a) Sulfur-containing amino acids (SCAAs) metabolism: Methionine (Met) is metabolized into homocysteine (Hcy) and hydrogen sulfide (H2S) via transsulfuration pathways. Elevated Hcy levels are linked to pro-inflammatory effects and upregulated matrix metalloproteinase (MMP-2/9). H2S exerts dual roles, with antioxidant and anti-inflammatory benefits, but also the potential to exacerbate neutrophil infiltration, impair vascular smooth muscle cell (VSMC) proliferation, and induce senescence, blunting compensatory aortic remodeling. (b) Arginine metabolism: Arginine serves as the substrate for endothelial nitric oxide synthase (eNOS), generating nitric oxide (NO), which mediates vasodilation and inhibits VSMC proliferation. Dysregulation involves the accumulation of asymmetric dimethylarginine (ADMA) due to diminished dimethylarginine dimethylaminohydrolase (DDAH) activity, arginase upregulation, and endothelial nitric oxide synthase (eNOS) uncoupling. De novo synthesis from citrulline via argininosuccinate synthase (ASS) and argininosuccinate lyase (ASL) links to glutamine (Gln), which offers protective effects against abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) by reducing VSMC apoptosis, M1 macrophage activation, oxidative stress, and extracellular matrix (ECM) degradation. (c) Gln and glutamate (Glu) metabolism: Gln, the most abundant amino acid in circulation, is synthesized mainly in skeletal muscle using circulating Glu as a substrate, while the liver produces Glu by deaminating Gln via glutaminase-2 (GLS2). A high plasma Gln/Glu ratio (GGR) was traditionally considered cardioprotective. However, GLS2 deficiency paradoxically elevates GGR yet accelerates atherosclerosis by promoting dysregulated ECM remodeling and arterial stiffness. (d) Branched-chain amino acids (BCAAs) metabolism: Aortic BCAAs catabolic defect results from the inhibitory phosphorylation of BCKD E1 subunit alpha (BCKDHA) by branched-chain α-ketoacid dehydrogenase kinase (BCKDK). This leads to oxidative stress damage and inflammatory cell infiltration via hyperactivated mTOR signaling, highlighting BCKDK and mTOR as potential therapeutic targets.
